Sort the Landforms: Plate Boundaries

Every photo below shows a real place, sourced from Wikipedia, Wikimedia Commons and GNS Science — a mountain, valley, cliff or fjord shaped by moving tectonic plates. Drag each photo card into the boundary bin where it belongs.

How to play: drag a card with your mouse or finger — or tap a card to pick it up, then tap a bin. Fill all three bins, then press Check my answers. Right answers lock in and reveal a fact. Wrong ones bounce back so you can try again. Stuck? Scroll down to the world map and tap a card's “Find it on the map” tag to see exactly where in the world it is.

Photo cards

Start here — drag these down into the bins

Divergent

Plates move APART

The crust stretches and cracks open. Look for rift valleys, gorges and new volcanic land in the gap.

Convergent

Plates move TOGETHER

Plates crash and crumple, or one dives under the other. Look for towering mountains and volcanoes.

Transform

Plates SLIDE SIDEWAYS

Plates grind past each other along a fault. Look for a straight line sliced through the land — offset valleys and scarps.

Field notes — the answer key

Facts unlock on each card when you sort it correctly. Here is the full set for checking and discussion.

A note for teachers: New Zealand sits on a bendy boundary that slides and squeezes, so its Southern Alps and Alpine Fault are sorted as transform (sideways grinding does most of the lifting there), while the Fiordland coast, where one plate dives offshore, is sorted as convergent. Doubtful Sound itself was carved by glaciers through mountains the boundary pushed up.

Photos were gathered from Wikipedia articles and Wikimedia Commons (plus GNS Science, New Zealand) and are shown at classroom size. Read more: Þingvellir · San Andreas Fault · Fiordland (home of Doubtful Sound)
